title: Trump Admin removes scientist in charge of climate change and global warming
description_short: Trump Admin removes scientist in charge of climate change and global warming
description_medium: The Trump administration reassigned Dr. Michael Kuperberg, director of the U.S. Global Change Research Program, on November 6, 2020. The program coordinates the National Climate Assessment, a major federal report on climate change. Kuperberg’s email indicated his detail at the program had ended and that he was returning to the Energy Department. The move became public the following week, amid other administration decisions affecting federal climate science.
description_long:
On November 6, 2020, the Trump administration ended Dr. Michael Kuperberg’s assignment as executive director of the U.S. Global Change Research Program and returned him to the Department of Energy. The USGCRP coordinates federal climate research and produces the National Climate Assessment, making Kuperberg’s role central to the government’s climate science work. The move was not publicly announced at the time; news reports surfaced early the following week after an automatic reply from his work email indicated that his detail at USGCRP had ended. Climate scientist Don Wuebbles told POLITICO that Kuperberg had received an email informing him of the reassignment.

The change came less than two months after the administration placed climate skeptic David Legates in a senior role at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The entry records a leadership change in a program responsible for federal climate assessments and places it alongside other personnel decisions on climate science. It does not establish that the National Climate Assessment was canceled or that its findings changed because of Kuperberg’s reassignment. Its documented consequence was that the program’s executive director was sent back to DOE during the final months of Trump’s first term.

title: Senate Jan 6 Report: Capitol Police Had 14 Intelligence Warnings Before Attack
description_short: Senate Jan 6 Report: Capitol Police Had 14 Intelligence Warnings Before Attack
description_medium: A bipartisan Senate report released in June 2022 found that the U.S. Capitol Police received at least 14 specific warnings of possible violence before the January 6, 2021 attack. The report described failures to act on intelligence across multiple agencies and said senior executive branch officials, including Trump advisers, had received threat briefings. It also recorded that Trump did not receive a morning intelligence briefing because he had not requested one.
description_long:
A bipartisan Senate report released June 7, 2022, examined intelligence and security preparations for the January 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol. It found that Capitol Police had received at least 14 specific intelligence warnings about possible violence but did not adequately prepare. The report described a broader intelligence failure involving several law-enforcement agencies. It also documented that senior executive branch officials, including advisers to President Donald Trump, had been briefed on the threat without prompting an increase in security.

According to testimony cited in the supplied account, Trump himself received no intelligence briefing on the morning of January 6 because he had not requested one. That distinction separates the information available to his advisers from what was briefed directly to the president. The Senate findings later informed the House January 6 Committee’s assessment of Trump’s inaction. The report documents warnings, briefing patterns, and preparedness failures; it does not by itself determine individual criminal liability. Its central finding was that threats were specific enough to warrant better preparation, yet agencies did not coordinate or respond adequately before the attack.

title: Trump: A majority of the Senate votes to convict Trump; Trump is acquitted anyways
description_short: Trump: A majority of the Senate votes to convict Trump; Trump is acquitted anyways
description_medium: On February 13, 2021, the Senate voted 57–43 to convict Donald Trump in his second impeachment trial over the January 6 attack. The vote was a majority but fell short of the two-thirds threshold required for conviction, so Trump was acquitted. After voting to acquit, Minority Leader Mitch McConnell said Trump was responsible for the attack but argued a former president could not be impeached.
description_long:
On the fifth and final day of Donald Trump’s second Senate impeachment trial, the Senate voted 57–43 to convict him of inciting the January 6 attack on the Capitol. A majority supported conviction, but the total was below the two-thirds threshold required by the Constitution, so Trump was acquitted. Seven Republicans joined all 50 Democrats in voting to convict.

After casting his own vote to acquit, Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell delivered a lengthy speech saying Trump was responsible for the attack. McConnell’s stated reason for acquittal was that he believed a president could not be impeached after leaving office. The timeline points out that McConnell had also blocked an earlier effort to begin the trial before Trump left office. The outcome ended the Senate proceeding without a conviction, despite the majority vote. This was Trump’s second acquittal by the Senate and left Congress without the formal sanction that a two-thirds conviction would have imposed. The entry records the vote and the stated conflict between McConnell’s assessment of responsibility and his constitutional rationale for acquittal.

description_long:

The timeline reports that Trump attorney Marc Kasowitz had donated $25,000 to Vance before the decision. Vance later returned that contribution, saying the refund would prevent speculation. The event is relevant because the decision involved close relatives of Donald Trump and an attorney representing them. title: Iran Retaliates: Ballistic Missile Strikes on US Bases in Iraq, 109 Troops TBI
description_short: Iran Retaliates: Ballistic Missile Strikes on US Bases in Iraq, 109 Troops TBI
description_medium: On January 8, 2020, Iran fired more than a dozen ballistic missiles at Al-Asad Air Base and another U.S. base in Erbil, Iraq, in retaliation for the U.S. killing of Iranian General Qassem Soleimani. Trump initially said no Americans were harmed. The Pentagon later reported that 109 U.S. service members had traumatic brain injuries. Trump publicly minimized the injuries as headaches, drawing criticism from injured troops and veterans.
description_long:
Iran launched more than a dozen ballistic missiles at two U.S. military installations in Iraq on January 8, 2020: Al-Asad Air Base and a base in Erbil. The attack was retaliation for the U.S. killing of Iranian General Qassem Soleimani. It marked the first time Iran had directly targeted U.S. forces with missiles, sharply raising the risk of further conflict between the countries. President Donald Trump initially said no Americans had been harmed.

The Pentagon later reported that 109 U.S. service members had been diagnosed with traumatic brain injuries from the strikes. Trump downplayed the injuries, describing them as headaches and questioning their seriousness. The contrast between his initial statement and the later Pentagon count became a central part of the public response. The episode followed a consequential U.S. military action and was followed by an Iranian strike on bases housing American personnel. The supplied account criticizes the administration’s escalation and deterrence strategy; this description records the missile attack, retaliation context, confirmed injuries, and Trump’s public response without asserting what alternative policy would have prevented the strike.

title: Take Back the Canal: Trump Vows to Seize Panama Canal on Inauguration Day
description_short: Take Back the Canal: Trump Vows to Seize Panama Canal on Inauguration Day
description_medium: In his January 20, 2025 inauguration speech, Donald Trump said the United States would take back the Panama Canal and falsely claimed China operated it. Panama’s foreign minister rejected the claim, and President José Raúl Mulino said canal sovereignty was not negotiable. Panama raised the threat at the United Nations Security Council. Secretary of State Marco Rubio then made Panama his first international stop, but acknowledged no agreement on transferring control was forthcoming.
description_long:
During his inauguration speech on January 20, 2025, Donald Trump vowed that the United States would “take back” the Panama Canal and claimed China was operating it. Panama’s Foreign Minister Javier Martínez-Acha responded that Panamanians alone operated the canal. President José Raúl Mulino called Trump’s statements false and said Panama’s sovereignty over the waterway was settled and non-negotiable. Panama formally brought the issue to the U.N. Security Council the following day, citing the U.N. Charter’s prohibition on threats against another country’s territorial integrity.

The dispute quickly became a matter of diplomacy. Secretary of State Marco Rubio made Panama his first international destination, but acknowledged that no deal to change control of the canal was forthcoming. Trump’s claim about Chinese soldiers at the canal was also rejected by Panama and became a source of nationalist backlash there. The entry documents a threat to take control, Panama’s defense of its sovereignty, and the diplomatic response. It does not describe a U.S. military action or an agreement to transfer the canal; control remained with Panama in the account provided.

title: Methane Fee Killed, Industry Given 18-Month Pollution Pass
description_short: Methane Fee Killed, Industry Given 18-Month Pollution Pass
description_medium: On March 14, 2025, Trump signed a law repealing the EPA’s methane waste emissions charge, which had imposed fees of $900 to $1,500 per excess ton from oil and gas operations. Congress passed the repeal in February under the Congressional Review Act. In July, EPA separately extended methane compliance deadlines by 18 months. The agency estimated the delay would allow millions of additional tons of methane and other pollutants to be emitted over the following decade.
description_long:
On March 14, 2025, Donald Trump signed Public Law 119-2, repealing the Environmental Protection Agency’s waste emissions charge for excess methane from oil and gas operations. The charge had ranged from $900 to $1,500 per excess ton. Congress approved the repeal in late February using the Congressional Review Act, removing a financial penalty established for high methane releases.

The EPA took a separate action on July 31, issuing an interim final rule that extended methane compliance deadlines by 18 months without first taking public comment. The agency’s fact sheet estimated that the delay would result in 3.8 million additional tons of methane emissions from 2028 through 2038, as well as 960,000 tons of volatile organic compounds and 36,000 tons of toxic air pollutants. The EPA compared the methane total to emissions from 25 million gasoline-powered vehicles driven for one year. The repeal and deadline extension were distinct decisions, but together reduced the immediate cost and timing pressure on oil and gas operators to address excess emissions. These are the agency’s projected effects, not measurements of emissions already released.

title: CHIP and Head Start Attacked: Children's Programs Slashed
description_short: CHIP and Head Start Attacked: Children's Programs Slashed
description_medium: The 2025 budget and reconciliation debate affected several children’s programs. The July 4 law imposed a 10-year pause on a Medicaid and CHIP enrollment rule, while research groups warned that work requirements and state cost changes could put children’s coverage at risk. Separately, Trump’s April draft HHS budget proposed eliminating Head Start funding for more than 500,000 children. These were different actions: enacted provisions and a budget proposal.
description_long:
The supplied account describes two separate 2025 actions affecting programs for children. The law signed July 4, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, imposed a 10-year moratorium on a Medicaid and CHIP eligibility and enrollment rule that had streamlined enrollment for more than 37 million children. Georgetown’s Center for Children and Families found that 21 states covering lawfully residing immigrant children through separate CHIP programs could face a doubled state share of costs unless they dropped coverage. The Commonwealth Fund estimated that one in five children could be at risk of losing Medicaid coverage under the bill’s work requirements.

Separately, a draft Health and Human Services budget from the Trump administration in April proposed eliminating all federal funding for Head Start, an early education program serving more than 500,000 vulnerable children. The proposal argued that Congress should not continue funding the program. A proposed budget is not itself an enacted cut, and the cited estimates describe potential risks rather than confirmed losses of coverage. The entry records the enacted enrollment-rule moratorium alongside a separate proposed Head Start elimination, clarifying their different status and the concerns raised by policy researchers.

title: Trump Asks NSA Director Mike Rogers to Deny Russia Investigation Evidence
description_short: Trump Asks NSA Director Mike Rogers to Deny Russia Investigation Evidence
description_medium: On May 22, 2017, Donald Trump contacted NSA Director Admiral Mike Rogers and asked him to publicly deny evidence of collusion between the Trump campaign and Russia. Rogers declined and documented the contact. Trump made a similar call to Director of National Intelligence Dan Coats that day. The contacts later became part of reporting and congressional testimony about presidential pressure on intelligence officials during the Russia investigation.
description_long:
On May 22, 2017, President Donald Trump separately contacted National Security Agency Director Admiral Mike Rogers and asked him to issue a public statement denying evidence of collusion with Russia. Rogers declined the request and documented the conversation. Trump also contacted Director of National Intelligence Dan Coats that day with a similar request. The simultaneous approaches to the heads of two intelligence agencies were later reported in the context of the federal investigation into Russian interference and possible links to the Trump campaign.

Both officials were cited in news accounts of the contacts in June 2017 and later testified to Congress. Former Director of National Intelligence James Clapper described the calls as an unprecedented intrusion on intelligence-community independence. The episode raised concerns about whether the president was trying to use intelligence agencies to counter a law-enforcement investigation that could affect him personally. The supplied account characterizes the contacts as coordinated pressure, but the factual core is the request, the officials’ refusals, and Rogers’s documentation. This entry does not claim the NSA director changed or falsified intelligence; the account says he did not issue the requested denial.
